stories.description: Streptococcus pneumoniae is a bacterial pathogen that causes life-threatening infections, including pneumonia and meningitis. These infections are commonly treated with antibiotics, but antibiotics are becoming less effective against S. pneumoniae over time because of changes in the pathogen that cause drug resistance. This phenomenon, called antimicrobial resistance, is resulting in significant health care costs and deaths around the world. In a new study published by Wiley in Advanced Science, researchers used artificial intelligence (AI) to identify approved drugs that may be effective against S. pneumoniae.

stories.title: What ancient Mars’s rocks reveal about its buried carbonate stores
stories.description: Mars once had abundant liquid water, yet orbiters and rovers have found far less carbonate rock than expected for a planet that may have had a thick, carbon dioxide-rich atmosphere. A new geochemical modelling study led by Chang-Chin Wang, with Professor Tomohiro Usui at JAXA and the University of Tokyo, and Associate Professor Mohit Melwani Daswani at ELSI, shows that the type of rock water reacts with, not just water itself, controls whether calcium/iron-rich or magnesium-rich carbonates form. Feldspar-rich rocks, increasingly detected on the Martian surface, readily produce the calcium/iron-rich carbonates seen in many locations. The simulations also show how percolating groundwater could be quietly burying carbonates underground, helping explain their apparent scarcity on the surface.

stories.title: Measuring emotions in skincare: exploring the hand as a model for facial application
stories.description: The application of cosmetic products creates a multisensory experience that can influence subjective and neurophysiological responses. This study explores differences between hand versus face applications. Thirty women participated in an experimental session combining subjective measures (questionnaires on valence, arousal, and product appreciation) and functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS), following application of either a serum or a no-product control to each area. Results show that when the serum is applied, there is no consistent difference between hand and face applications, either subjectively (valence, arousal, liking) or in terms of brain activity (prefrontal asymmetry measured by fNIRS). However, equivalence between application sites could not be formally established based on the present analyses. Conversely, in the absence of product, hand application is perceived as more pleasant than facial application. The presence of the serum was associated with more positive subjective evaluations and a more relaxed state, although this effect cannot be dissociated from differences in sensory properties such as fragrance, texture, or lubrication. These findings suggest that, within the limits of this exploratory study, no clear difference was detected between hand and face application under serum conditions in the present sample. Further research using more controlled designs and appropriate sensory controls is required before drawing any conclusions about the comparability of hand and face application for affective research purposes.
